## Principal findings
This study constitutes the first systematic cetacean survey conducted within the BGTW. Across 19 survey days, 126 on-effort sightings of two confirmed species were recorded, dominated by short-beaked common dolphin (*Delphinus delphis*). Encounter rate, expressed as sightings per unit effort, varied significantly among observation stations (Kruskal–Wallis: χ² = 14.13, df = 2, p = 0.001), being highest at Europa Point. The kernel density surface identified the southern tip of the peninsula as the principal area of elevated relative density. Detection-corrected density for the surveyed sectors was estimated at 4.66 individuals km⁻² (5 % CI: 2.81 - 7.73; CV: 0.26) (@tbl-pool_dens). Contrary to previously reported patterns [@olaya-ponzoneSpatioTemporalPatternsLimited2026], encounter rate was higher on the eastern than the western side of the study area (@fig-SPUE), identifying a previously undersampled sector. Beyond these results, the study provides a transferable, low-cost framework for systematic monitoring in geographically bounded territorial waters and establishes a baseline against which future spatial and temporal change can be assessed.

## Spatial heterogeneity
Cetacean occurrence within the surveyed sectors was strongly spatially structured, concentrating at the southern tip of the peninsula (Europa Point) rather than distributing evenly across the territory. The effort-standardised encounter rate (@fig-SPUE), the group-size-weighted kernel density surface (@fig-kde_map), and, critically, the detection-corrected density estimate all identified this southern concentration, the last preserving the Europa Point maximum across all tested truncation distances (**Table SXX**). This is consistent with De Stephanis et al. (2008), who linked cetacean distribution in the adjacent Strait to oceanographic and bathymetric structure rather than horizontal position, and with the canyon-associated aggregations reported by Olaya-Ponzone et al. (2025a) in the Bay of Algeciras.

The most plausible driver is enhanced local productivity: stronger currents around Europa Point promote upwelling and elevate primary production, creating favourable foraging conditions [@sanchez-garridoAlboranSeaCirculation2022] (Appendix G). Reduced disturbance may contribute secondarily, as the southern sector experiences less commercial bunkering than the Bay [@olaya-ponzoneVesselInducedBehavioural2025], though this cannot be tested here. A detectability artefact is unlikely to account for the pattern: although Europa Point was surveyed from the lowest platform (18 m a.s.l.), which compresses the effective detection range, the persistence of the Europa maximum in the detection-corrected estimates (**Table SXX**) indicates the concentration is not solely an observation effect. If confirmed across seasons, this localised concentration within an IMMA adjacent to a major traffic separation scheme implies that spatially targeted management, rather than a uniform BGTW-wide measure, is the appropriate conservation instrument.

## East–west contrast
The eastern–western asymmetry departs from previous work. Olaya-Ponzone et al. [-@olaya-ponzoneSpatioTemporalPatternsLimited2026; -@olaya-ponzoneMixedspeciesDolphinGroups2025] reported the highest detection rates within the Bay of Gibraltar and around the submarine canyon on the western side, whereas here per-unit-effort encounter rate was higher in the east. Two non-exclusive explanations are plausible. Observationally, the western vantage overlooks a bay heavily used for bunkering and anchorage, where moored vessels obstruct sightlines and the southerly viewpoint limits coverage of the northern bay, reducing detection reliability. Ecologically, the eastern sector has shallower bathymetry than the steeper western side [@sammartinoNumericalModelAnalysis2014; @azzellinoCetaceanResponseEnvironmental2017] (Appendix G) and, excepting the deep-water anchorage, lower vessel traffic, so it may represent a distinct, lower-disturbance habitat. Because the eastern sector has not previously been surveyed systematically, these explanations cannot yet be separated; the finding identifies it as a priority for targeted, repeated survey effort.

## Species composition and density in regional context
Two species were confirmed during systematic survey—short-beaked common dolphin (*Delphinus delphis*, n = 66) and fin whale (*Balaenoptera physalus*, n = 8)—alongside 50 sightings of dolphins that could not be identified to species (unidentified delphinids, n = 50). Common dolphins were the dominant taxon, consistent with its reported status in the wider Alboran Sea and Strait of Gibraltar [@canales-caceresDistributionBehaviourStriped2023; @gnoneCetaceansMediterraneanSea2023; @olaya-ponzoneMixedspeciesDolphinGroups2025]. The unidentified records reflect the constraints of shore-based observation, where range, sea state, and brief surfacing intervals often precluded confident assignment. Some sightings are likely common dolphins, with striped dolphins (*Stenella coeruleoalba*) and bottlenose dolphins (*Tursiops truncatus*) also plausible given their documented regional occurrence [@olaya-ponzoneMixedspeciesDolphinGroups2025].

Because no systematic survey has previously been conducted within the BGTW, these density estimates (@tbl-pool_dens) cannot be compared against an earlier local baseline; existing knowledge derives from opportunistic and ferry-based records that lack the effort information required for density estimation. They therefore constitute the first effort-corrected density values for the territory and should be treated as a provisional baseline rather than a point of comparison—their absolute magnitude interpreted cautiously given the sample-size and design constraints discussed below, their principal value lying in providing a reference against which future change can be assessed.

## Systematic vs. opportunistic sampling
The comparison with opportunistic records demonstrates the spatial bias inherent to platform-of-opportunity data. OBIS records of *Delphinus delphis* were strongly concentrated in the western bay, with only four in the eastern sector, whereas systematic surveys detected occurrence in the east at an encounter rate absent from the opportunistic record (@fig-obis). Because opportunistic recording tracks vessel routes and observer access rather than animal distribution, the existing record does not merely sample the eastern sector more sparsely but under-represents it systematically. A gap the present survey fills. Distribution inferences for the BGTW drawn from opportunistic data alone are therefore liable to directional spatial bias rather than reduced precision alone. The two approaches are best regarded as complementary rather than interchangeable: opportunistic and citizen-science recording offer broad temporal coverage, while systematic survey provides the effort-corrected, spatially balanced sampling required for density estimation [@bucklandIntroductionDistanceSampling2001; @dawsonDesignFieldMethods2008].

## Conservation implications
During surveys, recreational vessels were repeatedly observed approaching cetaceans, including fin whales, in breach of the Cetacean Protocol under the Gibraltar Marine Protection Regulations [-@zotero-item-2954], without observed on-water intervention. Vessel presence is known to disrupt cetacean behaviour [@hawkinsInteractiveBehavioursBottlenose2009; @neumannBehaviourEcologyCommon], boat strikes and evasive responses have been recorded locally [@olaya-ponzoneVesselInducedBehavioural2025]. The presence of fin whales, a large, slow-surfacing species, within a major traffic separation scheme compounds this into a ship-strike risk that protocol compliance alone may not mitigate. The observed non-compliance, together with the apparent absence of enforcement, indicates an implementation gap rather than a legislative one: adequate provisions exist, but their protective value depends on consistent enforcement and operator awareness. Targeted outreach and a visible enforcement presence at identified hotspots (notably the southern tip of the peninsula; @fig-kde_map), particularly during the high-traffic season, are therefore recommended (@fig-poster).

## Limitations {#limits}
Several constraints qualify these results. First, the land-based stations sampled only part of the BGTW, so density and abundance estimates apply to the surveyed sectors rather than the territory as a whole; because density was strongly spatially structured, they were not extrapolated to a territory-wide total. Second, per-station sample sizes fell below the level recommended for stable detection-function estimation [@bucklandIntroductionDistanceSampling2001; @bucklandDistanceSamplingMethods2015], requiring a single pooled function that assumes a common detection-function shape across stations—an assumption that introduces residual uncertainty beyond the reported confidence intervals. Third, the fixed observation stations depart from the randomly placed transects underlying design-based distance sampling [@keenDeterminingMarineMammal2020; @howeDistanceSamplingCamera2017], so estimates are conditional on the surveyed sectors rather than design-unbiased for them. Fourth, survey effort was restricted to daylight and favourable conditions, and covariates known to influence detectability (sea state, glare) and occurrence (depth, temperature) were recorded but could not be resolved at this sample size [@barlowEvaluatingBiasLinetransect2026; @azzellinoCetaceanResponseEnvironmental2017]; the estimates may therefore not represent occurrence across the full diel cycle, over which cetacean activity is known to vary [@cascaoTemporalPatternsAcoustic2020]. Finally, visual survey is biased toward larger and more conspicuous animals, likely under-representing small groups and inconspicuous surfacing [@giacomaAreLandBased2013]. These constraints, and possible mitigations, are examined in full in the Supplementary Material.

Notwithstanding these limitations, this study provides the first systematic, effort-corrected assessment of cetacean distribution within the BGTW. Occurrence was spatially structured and concentrated off the southern peninsula, and the eastern sector, ecologically notable yet almost absent from the opportunistic record, demonstrates that opportunistic data alone cannot substitute for design-based survey. The land-based approach offers a reproducible, low-cost framework for a data-poor IMMA under increasing pressure, and continued multi-season survey, integrated with photo-identification and environmental data, is needed to determine whether these patterns persist and to guide spatially targeted management.
